clue.text: Falter and start to become like Uriah Heep

indicators.note: the start of a word is its opening letter, so only the first letter of become is used

parts.note: Uriah Heep, the fawning clerk in Dickens's David Copperfield, calls himself 'umble, dropping the H of humble

explanation.surface: Someone stumbles and begins to turn into a fawning Dickens villain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'start to' takes just the B of 'become'. Uriah Heep is a Dickens character who keeps saying how 'umble' he is.
explanation.definitionFit: To bumble is to act or speak clumsily, stumbling over things, so it is a synonym of falter.

clue.text: Perhaps Eric's taken with African master

indicators.note: Eric's has taken with in, the name holding the abbreviation inside it

parts.note: Eric Bana is an Australian actor, so Eric is an example clue for his surname

explanation.surface: An actor called Eric is accompanied by a master from Africa.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Perhaps Eric' points to the actor Eric Bana; 'taken' puts W (with) inside BANA.
explanation.definitionFit: Bwana is a Swahili form of address meaning sir or boss, used in East Africa for a master.

clue.text: One protesting against disgraced Tory politician supporting Maggie's introduction

indicators.note: in a down clue the supporting piece sits underneath, so it is placed after the other
an introduction comes at the very beginning, so only the first letter of Maggie's is taken

parts.note: Jeffrey Archer, the Conservative politician and novelist, was jailed for perjury in 2001

explanation.surface: A protest is mounted against a fallen Tory who once backed Margaret Thatcher.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down answer 'supporting' means coming below, so ARCHER follows M. Jeffrey Archer is a British Conservative peer imprisoned for perjury; Maggie is Margaret Thatcher.
explanation.definitionFit: A person on a protest march is a demonstrator objecting to something.

clue.text: Assistance from US giving Ivan perhaps peace

parts.note: Ivan Lendl, the Czech-born tennis champion, is an Ivan, so his surname is clued by example
ease is peace of mind, freedom from worry

explanation.surface: Someone named Ivan is offering peace, said to be help coming from America.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ivan perhaps' calls for a famous Ivan: the tennis player Ivan Lendl.
explanation.definitionFit: Lend-Lease was the Second World War programme by which America supplied arms and goods to its allies.

clue.text: Ingenious upstart full-on in part

indicators.note: in part says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A bumptious newcomer goes all out, and is clever in some ways.
explanation.definitionFit: Artful describes someone clever and crafty in devising things, close to ingenious.

clue.text: Perhaps Führer and Balearics gutted about initially upsetting the French

annotationWithheld.why: Clue as held, 'Perhaps Führer and Balearics gutted about initially upsetting the French' (5) for RULER: 'Balearics gutted' gives BS, not R...R; the Fifteensquared blog parses R(U LE)R from Reichskanzler gutted, so the held text is garbled, too far off for an OCR fix, with no scan to confirm
annotationWithheld.clue: Perhaps Führer and Balearics gutted about initially upsetting the French

clue.text: Hot in finest woven fabric

indicators.note: Hot is put in the middle of the rearranged letters
woven means the letters of finest are interlaced into a new order

parts.note: H is the abbreviation for hot, as on a tap

explanation.surface: A garment is described as warm and made from the best woven cloth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'woven' rearranges FINEST and 'in' places H (hot) inside the new order.
explanation.definitionFit: Fishnet is an open mesh textile, best known in stockings.

clue.text: Double up over a Conservative buttering up

indicators.note: in a down clue over means the first piece sits on top of what follows
in a down answer up means the word for double is read from the bottom upwards

parts.note: dual means double, twofold
a Tory is a member of the British Conservative Party

explanation.surface: Someone doubles over and fawns over a Conservative.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up' turns DUAL into LAUD; 'over' in a down answer stacks it above A and TORY.
explanation.definitionFit: Laudatory means expressing praise, as flattery does, so it matches buttering up used adjectivally.

clue.text: Wayward state aid

parts.note: VA is the postal abbreviation for the US state of Virginia
a grant is a sum of money given as aid

explanation.surface: Public assistance from a government has gone astray.
explanation.walkthrough: 'state' is a US state here: VA, Virginia.
explanation.definitionFit: Vagrant can mean wandering or roaming without settled course, the sense of wayward.

clue.text: Shot of cavorting couples

indicators.note: cavorting means prancing about, so the letters of couples dance into a new order

explanation.surface: A photograph shows pairs dancing wildly.
explanation.definitionFit: A close-up is a type of camera shot taken at very short range.

clue.text: English vicar, not a radical, embracing spirit of a Christian Church

indicators.note: the shortened vicar holds the spirit inside it, as if hugging it
not tells us to remove the stated letters from the word vicar

parts.note: R is an abbreviation for radical
an angel is a spiritual being

explanation.surface: An English clergyman, no extremist, takes up the spirit of a church.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not a radical' strips A and R from the clergyman, and 'embracing' wraps the shortened word round the spirit, all after E for English.
explanation.definitionFit: Evangelic, like evangelical, describes Protestant churches stressing the gospel and personal conversion.

clue.text: Bart upset having eaten fruit after hard biscuit

indicators.note: the jumbled name takes the other pieces inside it, as if swallowing them
upset means knocked over, so the letters of Bart are rearranged
the fruit is placed after the letter for hard

parts.note: H is the abbreviation for hard, as on pencils
an olive is the fruit of the olive tree

explanation.surface: A boy named Bart, flustered, has had some fruit following a firm cracker.
explanation.walkthrough: 'upset' jumbles the name to BATR, and 'having eaten' takes H and the fruit inside it. A Bath Oliver is a plain, hard British dry biscuit, and the answer is also the surname of the Oliver Twist theme running through the across answers.
explanation.definitionFit: A Bath Oliver is a type of unsweetened dry cracker invented in Bath, eaten with cheese.

clue.text: Aussie shark getting into bath at intervals

indicators.note: at intervals means taking every other letter of the words into bath, starting from the second

explanation.surface: An Australian shark ends up in a bathtub now and then.
explanation.walkthrough: Take the even letters of INTOBATH. 'Noah' is Australian rhyming slang: Noah's ark for shark.
explanation.definitionFit: In Australian rhyming slang a biblical ark-builder's vessel rhymes with the fish, so his name serves for it.

clue.text: First of all consorts, attractive lady, albeit Sarkozy's third to be taken in

definitions.text: First of all consorts, attractive lady, albeit Sarkozy's third to be taken in

indicators.note: the single letter is taken into the row of initial letters
first of all asks for the opening letter of each of the following words in turn
the third letter of Sarkozy's is the one taken

explanation.surface: A glamorous presidential consort, whom Sarkozy himself married, is welcomed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'First of all' gives C, A, L, A from the next four words; 'to be taken in' puts R, Sarkozy's third letter, inside. Carla Bruni, singer and model, married French President Nicolas Sarkozy in 2008.
explanation.definitionFit: The whole clue describes the former model who became France's first lady through marrying the president.

clue.text: Wept about University College whenever harshly criticised

indicators.note: the word for wept goes about, surrounding, the other pieces

parts.note: cried means wept
UC is the abbreviation for University College
if can mean whenever, as in 'if it rains, we stay in'

explanation.surface: Someone cried over a university college whenever it was attacked.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' wraps the word for wept round the college letters and 'whenever'; 'harshly criticised' is the figurative sense of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To be crucified figuratively is to be savagely attacked or condemned in public.

clue.text: Swimming in a certain position in a race

indicators.note: the second in places the position word inside the word for race

parts.note: a nation is a people or race
at signals location, being in a particular place

explanation.surface: A competitor swims in a particular lane during a race.
explanation.walkthrough: 'race' looks like a contest but means a people; the second 'in' does the inserting.
explanation.definitionFit: Natation is a formal word for the act or art of swimming.

clue.text: Medicines or perhaps the ultimate in placebos

parts.note: in heraldry or is the gold colour, one example of a heraldic colour or tincture

indicators.note: the ultimate letter is the last one, so only the final letter of placebos is used

explanation.surface: Asking whether drugs are really just the best sugar pills.
explanation.walkthrough: 'or' looks like a link word but is the heraldic term for gold, one of the tinctures used on coats of arms.
explanation.definitionFit: Tinctures are medicinal preparations of a drug dissolved in alcohol.

clue.text: Trash opponents once you make dead centre

parts.note: bull is slang for nonsense or rubbish talk
in bridge South and East sit in opposing partnerships
ye is an old form of you

explanation.surface: Insult your rivals of old and you'll hit the middle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'opponents' is bridge: North-South play East-West, so S and E are opponents.
explanation.definitionFit: The bull's-eye is the exact centre of a target, so a shot there is dead centre.

clue.text: Play about in bottomless pool seeking this plant

indicators.note: the jumbled letters are placed inside the shortened pool
in a down clue the bottom is the last letter, which is removed

parts.note: a lido is a public open-air swimming pool

indicators.note: about means the letters of play are moved around

explanation.surface: Someone frolics in a bottomless pool hunting for a water plant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bottomless' drops the last letter of the pool to leave LID, and 'about' scrambles 'Play' to LYPA, which 'in' places inside.
explanation.definitionFit: A lily pad is the floating leaf of a water lily, standing for the plant itself.

clue.text: This city's French bread has crunchy crust

parts.note: naan or nan is a flat leavened Indian bread

indicators.note: a crust is the outside, so the first and last letters of crunchy are used

explanation.surface: A town's bakery boasts crusty French loaves.
explanation.walkthrough: 'crust' takes the first and last letters of 'crunchy', C and Y.
explanation.definitionFit: Nancy is a city in Lorraine, in north-eastern France.

clue.text: Tell a story about having bled on carpet

indicators.note: in a down clue on means placed on top of the next piece
about here means turned round, so the word for bled is read backwards

parts.note: ran means bled, as colours run in the wash
to carpet someone is to scold them, as is to rate them

explanation.surface: Someone recounts how they bled over the rug.
explanation.walkthrough: 'carpet' is a verb meaning to reprimand, as is the old verb rate; 'about' turns the word for bled round, and 'on' stacks it above in this down answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To narrate is to recount or relate events, as a storyteller does.

clue.text: Charge Clinton with initially behaving badly

indicators.note: initially picks out just the first letter of the next word, behaving

parts.note: ill can mean badly, as in ill-treated

explanation.surface: Accusing a US president of misconduct.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Clinton' is a second definition: Bill Clinton. 'initially' takes B from 'behaving', and ILL means badly.
explanation.definitionFit: A bill is a charge for goods or services owed; Bill is also the first name of President Clinton.

clue.text: Tool is grabbed by fool needing instruction

indicators.note: the short form of is is held inside the word for fool

parts.note: a twit is a silly person, a fool
is is shortened to the letter s, as in it's
drill is training or instruction, as in a fire drill

explanation.surface: An implement is seized by an idiot who needs teaching how to use it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'is' becomes 'S, as in it's; 'grabbed by' puts it inside TWIT to make TWIST.
explanation.definitionFit: A twist drill is a drill bit with helical grooves for boring holes.

clue.text: The ones in article about cartographers

indicators.note: about means the article goes round the abbreviation for the mapmakers

parts.note: the is the definite article
OS is Ordnance Survey, Britain's national mapping agency

explanation.surface: Those mentioned in a magazine piece about mapmakers.
explanation.walkthrough: OS stands for the Ordnance Survey, the UK's official map-maker.
explanation.definitionFit: Those is a pronoun meaning the people or things already mentioned or pointed out.

clue.text: Valid on appeal

parts.note: in cricket the leg side of the field is also called the on side
it is a dated term for sex appeal

explanation.surface: A legal argument is upheld when taken to a higher court.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on' is a cricket term: the leg side is the on side. 'appeal' is IT, as in sex appeal.
explanation.definitionFit: Legit is informal for legitimate, lawful or genuine.

clue.text: Clamp it properly to bear support for mine

indicators.note: to bear means to carry or hold, so the words clamp it properly hold the answer inside them

explanation.surface: Instruction to fix a clamp correctly so it can take weight in a mine.
explanation.definitionFit: A pit prop is a wooden or metal post holding up the roof in a coal mine.

clue.text: Get no time on Scottish Island to settle

indicators.note: in an across clue on means attached after the island

parts.note: Arran is an island in the Firth of Clyde, off western Scotland

indicators.note: no means the abbreviation for time is removed from get

explanation.surface: Get to a Scottish island to settle down, with no time to spare.
explanation.walkthrough: 'no time' takes T out of 'Get' to leave GE; in an across answer 'on' puts it after the island. Arran lies in the Firth of Clyde.
explanation.definitionFit: To arrange matters is to organise or settle them.

clue.text: Screen printer ultimately succeeding to partially limit exposure

indicators.note: succeeding means following on, so the single letter is placed after

parts.note: in photographic printing to dodge is to shade part of the print so that area gets less light

indicators.note: ultimately points to the final letter of printer

explanation.surface: A screen printer finally manages to reduce exposure in places.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Screen printer' reads as one trade but splits: 'Screen' is the definition, and a dodger is the canvas screen on a ship's bridge.
explanation.definitionFit: A dodger is a protective canvas shield on a ship's bridge or a yacht's cockpit against spray.

clue.text: A wind coming up

parts.note: wind can mean scent, as when a hound gets wind of its quarry

explanation.surface: A breeze rising.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wind' is a smell, as in 'get wind of'.
explanation.definitionFit: An ascent is a rising or climb, the act of going up.
